facts.fact: The Uganda Bureau of Statistics draws its 2024 counts from NIRA's Mobile Vital Records System, in which 498,439 live births of all ages (51,527 of them under one year, against 1,515,437 expected births, 3.4%) and 22,182 deaths (8,921 within a year of occurrence, 3.9% of expected) were registered in 2024.

The report describes the Mobile Vital Records System as the system used by the National Identification and Registration Authority, which registers births and deaths under the Registration of Persons Act 2015 on notifications created by the Ministry of Health.

The bureau attributes the 2022 peak in birth registration (175,328 under-one births, 10.8% completeness) to support for civil registration under the World Bank's URMCHIP project and UNICEF support to birth registration in 38 focus districts; it names no domestic budget line for the system.

Under-one births registered in the Mobile Vital Records System fell from 108,655 in 2023 to 51,527 in 2024 (completeness 6.6% to 3.4%) and deaths registered within a year from 17,597 to 8,921 (5.9% to 3.9%), on the Uganda Bureau of Statistics' figures.

slug: 2020-01-01 Maintaining civil registration amid COVID-19 - Uganda's mobile notification system (IDRC)

facts.fact: The brief states that NIRA, the registration agency, operates the central civil register using the MVRS web application, having taken it over from the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, which developed it in 2011; the brief gives no date for this, so its 2020 publication year is used.

The brief states that births are notified and registered in the MVRS and that death registration uses the same process and system, with about 83,200 birth events recorded in January-August 2020 and only 2,099 deaths registered from January 2018 to August 2020, on the MVRS dashboards.

The brief states that a paper notification form completed at a registration office, health facility or in the community is entered into the web-based MVRS at district offices and health facilities, and that every notification entered and registered there is recorded directly in the central NIRA register, with approval by the registrar at head office or a designated district office.
The brief states that as of 2020 MVRS is used in 112 of 135 districts and in 222 of the 5,230 health facilities that handle births; it elsewhere speaks of 122 districts where MVRS is used.

The brief states that the lockdown imposed on 31 March 2020 and extended to the end of June closed all district civil registration offices, officers entering events into MVRS from home, and that the birth events NIRA recorded electronically in January-August 2020 were 21 per cent of those of the same period in 2019.

slug: 2019-01-01 Snapshot of CRVS Systems of Uganda (IDRC Centre of Excellence)

facts.fact: The snapshot, from a questionnaire NIRA completed in January 2019, states that NIRA, an authority under the Ministry of Internal Affairs, registers births and deaths and that their information is entered into the national database.
The snapshot states that a strategic plan for the improvement of CRVS systems has not been developed, Uganda having completed only a baseline survey, on NIRA's questionnaire of January 2019.

The snapshot states that information on budgetary requirements and allocations was not available, and lists World Bank, Global Financing Facility and UNICEF support to NIRA, on NIRA's questionnaire of January 2019.

The snapshot states that the registration of births and deaths is paper-based at the lowest registration centres and that the information is entered into the national database at regional level, on NIRA's questionnaire of January 2019.

The snapshot states that registration of births and deaths is paper-based at all of the lowest registration centres, that the information is entered into the national database at regional level, and that CDs and flash discs carry it from local centres to the next higher office, on NIRA's questionnaire of January 2019.

The snapshot states that all local registration offices have computers, beside a count of 152 district-level births and deaths registration offices, of which it puts 133 in rural and 19 in urban areas, while registration at the lowest centres stays on paper, on NIRA's questionnaire of January 2019.

note: Read from the artefact PDF. The snapshot describes the Mobile Vital Record System only as mobile notification of births, so it is entered as notification here and gives no fact; the civil facts are on the unnamed national database. For exchange: a NIN is issued at birth registration, yet the two NIRA systems are not electronically linked (January 2019). The office percentages the PDF prints (14 and 86 per cent) do not match its counts of 19 and 133 of 152.

facts.fact: The World Bank states that the MVRS project, which followed in 2011 and ran with UNICEF support over 2013-2015, computerised the birth registration process, and that death registration, though provided for in the MVRS software, was not made operational; URSB annual reports for 2013-14 to 2015-16 give 2,030,355 births registered.

The World Bank states that MVRS used web-based transmission of data and mobile phone messaging to computerise birth registration, digitising data recording and transmission at connected ('online') registration points whose activity could be seen centrally; it dates this to the project period 2011-2015.

The World Bank states that MVRS had 202 connected registration points, a modest portion of the more than 1,400 sub-counties and 345 health facilities (as of July 2012) where registration was possible, and was reportedly installed in 77 districts (NIRA and Plan International 2017); the count itself is not dated, so the end of the project period is used.

The World Bank reports the MVRS registrations from the annual reports of the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, which managed all civil registration from 2004 until the transfer to NIRA on 1 January 2016.
The World Bank describes MVRS as a UNICEF-supported project, implemented over 2013-2015, and gives no domestic budget line for it; URSB annual reports give no separate civil registration expenditure.

The World Bank states that the civil register consisted, and under the 2015 law still consists, of the manually made, paper-based registers kept by registrars across the country (more than 10 million records), beside about 3-5 million entries in the digital systems MVRS and CRIMS; the diagnostic was made between November 2017 and June 2018.
facts.system: civil register for births and deaths

facts.fact: The World Bank states that responsibility for birth, death and adoption registration passed from URSB to the National Identification and Registration Authority on 1 January 2016, under the Registration of Persons Act 2015.

facts.fact: The World Bank cites NIRA's Strategic Plan 2017/18-2019/20, subtitled as scaling up civil registration and vital statistics, with a budget of USh 624.2 billion over three years, and adds that a costed national CRVS strategic plan will also be critical; it does not say the plan names a registration system.

facts.fact: The World Bank states that the Government of Uganda, the World Bank, UNICEF and Plan International cover half of NIRA's planned USh 624.2 billion for 2017/18-2019/20, that the medium-term allocation is USh 269 billion (43 per cent of the need), and that the Bank's Reproductive, Maternal and Child Health Services Improvement Project is funding NIRA to scale up birth and death registration; the budget covers the national ID as well as civil registration.

slug: 2017-01-01 AU - Report on the Status of Civil Registration and Vital Statistics in Africa
note: A continental report of aggregate counts from the October 2016 APAI-CRVS self-reported monitoring round; Uganda appears only in the annex's composite score bands (digitization 80-100%, legal framework 50-64%, infrastructure and resources 50-64%, planning and coordination 35-49%, registration process 35-49%, overall 50-64%), which state nothing about any one aspect and name no system.

facts.fact: The Registration of Persons Act, assented to and commenced in part on 26 March 2015, establishes the National Identification and Registration Authority as a body corporate under the minister for internal affairs and gives it the function of registering births and deaths (section 5(1)(d)); the excerpt held names no civil registration system.

About a copyright management system; the Registrar General named is the head of the Uganda Registration Services Bureau speaking on copyright and business registration, and nothing concerns the registration of births or deaths.

The statistics bureau's budget performance to end December 2025: it lists a Civil Registration and Vital Statistics report and the Vital Statistics Report 2024 as produced and disseminated, which are statistical publications; nothing on how or where births and deaths are registered, and no registration system is named.

An excerpt of the census report that stops in chapter 2, before the birth registration and death registration sections its contents list; the held text gives only SDG 16.9.1 (10.3% of children under five registered with a birth certificate, May 2024), a share of births and not of offices, and names no registration system.

facts.fact: The Registration of Persons Act, assented to on 26 March 2015, makes the National Identification and Registration Authority, a body corporate under the minister for internal affairs, responsible for registering births and deaths (section 5(1)(d)), with a registration officer in charge of each registration area entering every notified birth in the register (section 29(1)); Parts V and VI on births and deaths commenced on 1 January 2016, and the Act names no civil registration system.
